beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Someone's about to ask whether Claude needs training to do earnings analysis. Wrong question. Training rewrites the model's weights — nobody's doing that for one report. Anthropic built a briefing layer instead: a file Claude reads before it acts. Same model, tighter job.

beats.narration_text: A Claude skill is a folder with one markdown file inside it — SKILL.md. That's the whole mechanism. No code, no compiled artifact, no training pass. Just prose Claude reads before it acts. This one's called earnings-analysis. The design bet is honest: if the model can already read documents, the fastest way to specialize it is to write down what you want and hand it that document every time.

Inside SKILL.md there's a Steps section. Claude reads step one, does it, reads step two, does it — straight down the list. No branching unless a step explicitly calls for one. That linearity is a choice: it trades flexibility for something you can actually predict. Same input, same steps, same shape of output — every time.

production_viz.label: READ, THEN EXECUTE
production_viz.caption: linear — no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: The scope is stated plainly at the top of the file: one job — turn a company's quarterly numbers into a written earnings update. Eight to twelve pages. One to three tables. Eight to twelve charts. That's the whole brief. Anything outside those numbers isn't part of what this skill does. The narrowness is the point: scope creep is how outputs become unpredictable, so the file just refuses to have opinions about anything else.

So the carry-out: a skill is a file, not training. It doesn't make Claude smarter — Claude's already got the intelligence. What the file gives it is a fixed job, done the same way, every time. That repeatability is the actual product.

props.quote: A Claude skill is a file, not training. It doesn't make Claude smarter — it gives Claude one job, done the same way, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I want a professional equity-research earnings update — eight to twelve pages, three to five thousand words, covering beat-or-miss, updated estimates, and the revised thesis. Read the earnings-analysis skill first, and walk me through what you'll do before you do it. That last clause is the important one. Asking the model to explain the plan before it runs surfaces the actual constraints the file imposes — you find out what the skill will and won't do while there's still time to correct course.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It asks the model to place skills against two neighbors — fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation — and force the trade-offs into the open, so you can see when each is actually the right tool. Go deeper: pick a repeatable knowledge-work job you already do — a weekly report, a code review, an incident postmortem — and draft a SKILL.md for it, with a Steps section a colleague could follow. Writing one teaches you what the job actually is.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how Claude 'skills' work as a specialization mechanism — plain-language markdown files (SKILL.md) that Claude reads before acting on a job, rather than fine-tuning or retraining the model. Compare skills against two neighbors: (1) fine-tuning, which rewrites the model's weights, and (2) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which injects retrieved context at query time. For each of the three, explain what actually changes in the pipeline, what it optimizes for, what it sacrifices, and one job it's the right tool for. End with a rule of thumb for choosing between them when I want a repeatable, narrowly-scoped output like an earnings update.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: pick a repeatable knowledge-work job you already do — a weekly report, a code review, an incident postmortem — and draft a SKILL.md for it, with a Steps section a colleague could follow. What did writing it force you to notice about the job that you didn't already know?
